name: Social Gospel
summary: The Social Gospel is the early twentieth-century Protestant reform movement that treated the Kingdom of God as a task for this world and held that churches must remake industrial society by Christian ethics. Its leaders (Washington Gladden, Walter Rauschenbusch) backed labor unions, a living wage, workplace protections, progressive inheritance taxation, public ownership of natural monopolies and municipal services, and a democratized politics, while rejecting absolute private property rights and favouring evolutionary rather than violent change.
scope: The American Protestant Social Gospel of about 1870 to 1918 as the defining encyclopedia entries (s1, s2) present it: Gladden and Rauschenbusch as its founding theologians (named in both), with the 1908 Federal Council Social Creed as its programme. Answers rest on Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis and Christianizing the Social Order, Gladden's Tools and the Man, and the Creed. It excludes later movements it influenced (Christian realism, the civil rights movement, liberation theology), British Christian socialism, Catholic social teaching, and the Prohibition politics that some denominations pursued.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Rauschenbusch writes that workingmen must have the right to bargain collectively and that public opinion and the law must uphold that demand; the Social Creed's reception is described as affirming labor's right to bargain collectively.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Rauschenbusch wants the law to give trades legal recognition, jurisdiction over their members' qualifications, collective bargaining and joint conciliation tribunals with employers, which is close to but not explicitly bargaining bodies that set wages.

direct-votes.rationale: Rauschenbusch welcomes direct legislation (initiative and referendum) as a way of socializing the machinery of government, though he does not argue that all major laws should be decided by popular vote.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1908 Social Creed stands for equal rights and complete justice for all men in all stations of life, and Rauschenbusch holds that democracy gives political and economic expression to the Christian conviction of the worth of every man.

family-wage.rationale: Rauschenbusch says the living wage must be enough for the father of an average family to keep a sanitary home, feed and school the children and insure against sickness and age; the 1908 Social Creed asks a living wage as a minimum in every industry.

gradual-change.rationale: Rauschenbusch bases hope on evolutionary advance and warns that force is the longest way, but also says the doctrine of gradualness may be overworked and urges 'go slow, but hurry up'.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Rauschenbusch's goal is to give back to the community the unearned ingredients in rent and profit and to stop unearned incomes, so that income follows useful work.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Rauschenbusch argues for socializing water, transit, gas and electric supply, and urges cities to supply milk, ice, coal and drugs as vital community needs not to be left to profit-seekers.

more-religion-public.rationale: The movement's defining thesis, in Rauschenbusch's title and argument, is that Christianity should remake the social, economic and political order; the encyclopedia describes the social gospel as applying Christian ethics to social problems.

production-for-use.rationale: Rauschenbusch states that industry ought to exist for the support of life but actually exists to make money, and that all the powers of Christianity should react against this perversion.

property-franchise.rationale: Rauschenbusch calls restricting the suffrage on property lines a remnant of the feudal system of granting political power to those who already hold economic power.

property-fundamental.rationale: Rauschenbusch writes that neither religion, ethics nor law recognizes an absolute private property right and that private property must cease where it endangers the public welfare.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Rauschenbusch teaches that all property is a trust and the owner a steward, that ethics makes the moral title depend on the service rendered, and that private property exists because it is for the public good; Gladden calls property communion with God through the material world, with duties to fellow men.

public-ownership.rationale: Rauschenbusch holds that the natural monopolies (railways, transit, power, telephone, and control of mineral and water-power resources) are the irreducible minimum that must come under public ownership, and that a business employing thousands is in truth public, but he does not call for general public ownership of all major industries.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: In Christianizing the Social Order (chapter on the conservation of life) Rauschenbusch demands a living wage enough for the father of an average family and minimum wage boards in every state, and attacks the courts' 'freedom of contract' doctrine that blocks a legal minimum wage.

recall-officials.rationale: Rauschenbusch lists direct nominations, direct legislation and the recall among the measures that democratize government and he looks to them to cleanse politics.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Rauschenbusch wants safety, hours, wage and accident standards imposed on employers by law and monopolies publicly supervised or owned, though he calls mere supervision a halfway house.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Gladden holds that organized labor has the right to strike for better pay or conditions, a last resort short of violence, which sits against a law restricting strikes; Rauschenbusch likewise wants law to uphold labor's demands.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Rauschenbusch treats the protective tariff as an example of privilege, a device to relieve certain industries of competition at the people's cost.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Rauschenbusch calls a progressive inheritance tax one of the most approved ways of resocializing large fortunes and says it should be applied far more thoroughly than hitherto; the encyclopedia credits Gladden with calling for inheritance taxation.

unions-good.rationale: Rauschenbusch calls the organizations of labor indispensable to the rise of the working class and Gladden holds that organization of labor is necessary under the wage system to the preservation of the laboring class and the welfare of society; the encyclopedia accounts record the movement's backing for unions.

war-builds-character.rationale: Rauschenbusch writes that war drains the life of nations by killing off the capable, and that the church has not yet turned its moral force against war as such, which treats war as a harm rather than a source of national character.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Rauschenbusch says the perpetuation of great fortunes is dangerous to the social order, and calls enormous inequalities of property an institutionalized denial of Christian equality that democracy must melt down.

women-suffrage.rationale: Rauschenbusch calls the agitation for woman's suffrage one of the final steps of woman's ascent and says it removes one of the last remnants of patriarchal autocracy by giving women their own political rights.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Rauschenbusch argues for economic democracy in which employers give up autocratic power and workers have a voice, though he sets this in terms of industrial democracy to come rather than a specified vote on company management.

notes: Statement bank read in full (598 statements). Themes searched in Rauschenbusch's Christianizing the Social Order and Christianity and the Social Crisis, Gladden's Tools and the Man and the 1908 Creed: wages and hours, unions and strikes, taxation (inheritance, land, tariffs, indirect taxes), property, public ownership, democracy and suffrage, revolution and class struggle, race, war and peace, prisons, alcohol, sexuality, education, immigration, technology and environment. Most of the bank is not addressed by these sources and stays null; the Social Gospel was an economic and ethical reform movement and its own texts say little on foreign policy, security, identity, ecology or technology. The movement's Prohibition campaign and its pre-war wartime stances were not used (denominational campaigns, not stated tenets). Several answers rest on Rauschenbusch alone because Gladden's and the Creed's texts are shorter; the encyclopedia entries confirm both as defining figures.
